questions.q: What does HHL actually output when solving Ax = b, and why does that matter?
options: A quantum state |x> whose amplitudes are proportional to the entries of x, not a classical list of the N solution values -- so usefulness depends on what you need to do with x next
The exact classical vector x, printed out as N floating-point numbers, just like a classical solver
Only the matrix A's eigenvalues, not any information about x
A randomly sampled approximate guess at a single entry of x, with no further structure
questions.explain: HHL's output is a quantum encoding of the solution, not a classical readout -- getting specific classical numbers out requires further measurement, as the lesson's third caveat explains.

questions.q: How does HHL's claimed runtime compare to the best classical sparse-system methods, in the dimension N?
options: HHL scales roughly as O(log(N) . s^2 . kappa^2 / eps), vs. classical methods like conjugate gradient scaling roughly as O(N . s . kappa) -- an exponential improvement in N alone
HHL and classical methods both scale as O(N), with no meaningful difference
HHL scales as O(N^2), worse than classical methods in every case
HHL scales as O(sqrt(N)), a quadratic improvement similar to Grover's algorithm
questions.explain: The headline log(N) vs. N comparison is where HHL's apparent exponential advantage comes from -- but the lesson's caveats explain why this comparison alone overstates the real-world picture.

questions.q: Why can state preparation of b silently cancel out HHL's log(N) advantage?
options: Loading an arbitrary N-dimensional vector into a quantum state can itself cost O(N) operations in general, which would erase the exponential gain before the algorithm even begins
State preparation is always free and never affects the overall runtime
Because b must always be measured classically first, which takes zero time
Because A, not b, is the only input that needs to be loaded into a quantum state
questions.explain: HHL's speedup assumes b can be loaded efficiently; without that assumption holding, preparing |b> can cost as much as O(N), removing the exponential advantage over classical methods.

questions.q: Why does a large condition number kappa hurt HHL's advantage specifically, according to the runtime formula given in this lesson?
options: HHL's runtime scales as kappa^2, while classical conjugate gradient scales only linearly in kappa, so poorly conditioned systems (common in real discretized or noisy data) shrink or erase HHL's advantage exactly where real systems are hardest
Condition number has no effect on either HHL's or classical methods' runtime
A large kappa makes classical methods slower but has zero effect on HHL's runtime
Kappa only affects the sparsity s, not the runtime directly
questions.explain: Because HHL's cost grows as kappa^2 versus classical's linear kappa dependence, HHL's relative advantage is weakest exactly in the ill-conditioned regime where real-world systems are often most numerically difficult.

questions.q: What's specifically wrong with the claim 'HHL exponentially speeds up solving any system of linear equations'?
options: The exponential advantage only holds under three conditions -- efficient state preparation of b, a favorable (small) condition number, and a readout need limited to an aggregate quantity rather than the full vector x -- so 'any' and 'exponentially' both overstate the real, conditional result
HHL never provides any speedup over classical methods under any circumstance
HHL only works for non-Hermitian, dense matrices, which makes 'any system' technically correct
The claim is entirely correct as stated, with no caveats needed
questions.explain: The three caveats in this lesson -- state preparation, condition number sensitivity, and readout cost -- are exactly why HHL's exponential speedup is conditional and narrow, not universal, making 'any' and 'exponentially' both misleading as stated.
